records.subject: business
records.title: Break-even Sensitivity and Margin of Safety
records.learningGap: Learners may perform isolated break-even and margin-of-safety calculations without seeing how changing selling price, fixed costs or variable cost per unit changes contribution, moves the revenue/cost intersection and can reverse a decision.
records.overlapCheck: This packet narrows the former Cost, Scale and Break-even Decisions record to one-product break-even sensitivity. It excludes broad cost classification, average-cost work, economies/diseconomies of scale, capacity systems and supplier/product comparisons. The current deployed live set has no Business Studies break-even lab; adjacent percentage, tariff, throughput, feasible-region and similarity-scale mechanics are not reproduced.

syllabusObjectives.claim: concept of break-even
complete or amend a simple break-even chart
interpret a break-even chart
calculate break-even output
define, calculate and interpret the margin of safety
use break-even analysis to help make decisions: effect of changes in price, changes in fixed costs, changes in variable cost per unit
limitations of break-even analysis

book.label: Cambridge IGCSE Business Student's Book, Sixth Edition (2025), supporting 0264/0774/7081 from 2027; bounded break-even treatment only, not syllabus authority
book.excerptEvidence: Printed p.252: amend the chart when costs or selling price change; contribution per unit and break-even-output formula. Printed p.253: margin of safety and actual output minus break-even output. Printed p.254: price, fixed-cost and variable-cost sensitivity for decisions. Printed p.255: assumptions and limitations.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Business 0264 syllabus 2027-2029
references.teachingConnection: Authoritative Section 4.4.3 outcomes on PDF page 18, including break-even charts, break-even output, margin of safety, sensitivity decisions and limitations.
references.locator: Local syllabus PDF p.18, Section 4.4.3.

references.title: Calculate a Break-Even Point in Units and Dollars
references.teachingConnection: Supports contribution margin, fixed and variable costs, break-even output and the relevant-range assumptions that bound a one-product model.

references.title: Perform Break-Even Sensitivity Analysis for a Single Product under Changing Business Situations
references.teachingConnection: Section 3.3's single-variable and multiple-variable cases show contribution, break-even and operating income recalculating when price, variable cost or fixed cost changes.
references.locator: Section 3.3 headings `Changing a Single Variable` and `Changing Multiple Variables`; inspect the worked selling-price, variable-cost and fixed-cost cases.

transferableMechanism.control: Change one price, variable-cost or fixed-cost assumption.
transferableMechanism.stateChange: Contribution and break-even evidence recalculate.
transferableMechanism.feedback: The lab transfers this into moving revenue/total-cost lines, their intersection, profit/loss region and margin of safety in one persistent graph.

references.title: Break-even: drag the price
references.teachingConnection: The Break-even Explorer presents price as a direct control and keeps contribution and break-even count visible in the same model.
references.locator: Break-even Explorer default: price $35, variable cost $20, fixed costs $24,000, contribution $15, break-even 1,600 units and sales at that count $56,000. The page presents a price control and explains that raising price increases contribution and lowers break-even output.

transferableMechanism.control: Directly vary the represented price/revenue relationship, with an equivalent keyboard path.
transferableMechanism.stateChange: The price/contribution readout and break-even count change; the graph's revenue relationship moves.
transferableMechanism.feedback: The learner sees the changed graph and can revise a proceed/revise decision from the visible break-even and margin state.

interaction.learnerAction: Commit to a proceed-or-revise decision at a planned output, then directly drag price, variable-cost-per-unit, fixed-cost and planned-output handles on one persistent break-even graph; inspect contribution, moved lines/intersection, profit/loss and margin of safety, and revise the decision after a consequential change.
interaction.visibleChange: Selling price changes revenue slope and contribution; variable cost per unit changes total-cost slope and contribution; fixed costs move the total-cost intercept; the break-even intersection, profit/loss regions, planned-output margin interval and decision evidence update together.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Contribution per unit equals selling price minus variable cost per unit; break-even output equals fixed costs divided by contribution; margin of safety equals planned/current output minus break-even output. Price, fixed-cost and variable-cost changes can therefore alter the break-even intersection and reverse a decision within stated assumptions.
modelLimitations: One product; all planned units are sold.
Selling price and variable cost per unit are constant over the displayed range; fixed costs and lines are treated as constant/linear.
No demand response, inventory, multiple products, capacity expansion or economies/diseconomies of scale; not a real-business forecast or advice.

records.distinctGap: A directly manipulated, persistent cost-volume graph makes the causal chain from price/fixed cost/variable cost per unit to contribution, intersection, margin of safety and a revised decision visible; it is not a spreadsheet or a prepared case selector.
records.revisedDirection: Narrow this from the former broad cost/scale workbench to one directly operated break-even graph: price, fixed cost and variable cost per unit change contribution, move the revenue/cost intersection and margin of safety, and can change the decision. Keep broad cost classification, economies/diseconomies of scale, capacity effects and dashboard-style controls out of scope.

assessment.summary: Rank 1. Build now after narrowing the broad cost/scale record. Scores: curriculum importance 2; concept strength 2; authentic experimental potential 2; resource quality 2; overlap risk 2; need for interactivity 2. The exact 0264 §4.4.3 and local book evidence support one persistent graph-based sensitivity loop; broad cost classification and economies/diseconomies of scale are deliberately excluded. Direct sensitivity, retained graph state and decision revision make this the only currently verified Business packet target.

interaction.visibleChange: Separate survival, growth, profit or market-share evidence and stakeholder consequences update; conflicts stay visible rather than collapsing into a popularity score.

The Oilco case and objective/stakeholder diagram already make the trade-off explicit without arbitrary weights.

reasons why businesses succeed or fail, e.g. management skills, availability of finance, suitability of product, demand for products, changes in the economy, level of competition

references.teachingConnection: Firm characteristic, measure, geography and time controls update charts/maps/tables, but do not operate a business growth choice through its consequences.

interaction.learnerAction: Compare supplied firms using employees, value/volume of sales or output and capital employed, justify a size measure, then choose remaining small, internal growth, horizontal integration or vertical integration and run a review period.
interaction.visibleChange: Rankings change with the measure; growth updates reach, control, finance/management load and integration problems; later evidence can expose success, failure risk or a rational case for staying small.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Size is multidimensional and profit is not a measure; growth methods have conditional purposes, benefits and problems, so growth is not always best.

records.distinctGap: The size/growth judgments are curriculum-valid, but no standalone causal system is verified.

Need for interactivity 0: tables and cases suffice. Tier judgment: human-review; not a future packet preference.

records.revisedDirection: Do not packet this as a size-and-growth dashboard. Census BDS filters real data and can change comparisons, but does not let a learner choose internal, horizontal or vertical growth or remaining small and observe success, failure or management problems. The book’s size-measure and growth cases remain the appropriate treatment.

references.title: The Production Possibility Frontier Game
references.teachingConnection: Verified transferable affordance: reallocate a fixed workforce between two outputs or change the production process → the pair of feasible outputs and plotted frontier change → the forgone next-best output and shifted feasible set make opportunity cost visible; the Business adaptation must not teach PPF analysis.
references.locator: Timed two-output worker-allocation activity followed by the Excel frontier plot.

interaction.learnerAction: Allocate limited land, labour and capital under one enterprise decision, choose a product/service stage, predict selling-price and bought-in-input effects, then compare the chosen option with the next-best feasible alternative.
interaction.visibleChange: Allocation changes output, bought-in cost, selling price and added value; the rejected option remains visible as opportunity cost; each stage has independent activity-sector and ownership-sector tags.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Businesses combine factors under scarcity, added value changes with selling price or bought-in costs, opportunity cost is the next-best alternative forgone, and activity sector differs from ownership sector.

records.distinctGap: The current record joins several introductory definitions that do not require one persistent interactive state.

assessment.summary: Curriculum importance 2: exact §§1.1–1.2 and book evidence are complete. Concept strength 0: the record combines disconnected introductory outcomes. Authentic experimental potential 1: the PPF activity supports opportunity cost only and is out of scope. Resource quality 2: authoritative evidence is available but incomplete as design direction. Overlap risk 2: no deployed lab covers it. Need for interactivity 0: diagrams, examples and classifications suffice. Tier judgment: human-review; not a future packet preference.

records.revisedDirection: Do not packet the current four-part allocation workbench. The PPF game authentically links fixed-resource reallocation to forgone output, but PPF analysis is explicitly outside the bounded 0264 treatment and it does not demonstrate added value or activity/ownership-sector classification. Use the book diagrams, examples and classification work unless a narrower non-PPF relationship is later justified.

records.subject: business
records.title: Cash-flow Forecast and Resilience
records.learningGap: Learners may complete a cash-flow table mechanically but not understand how timing causes a profitable business to run out of cash or how each short-term remedy protects one balance while creating another consequence.
records.overlapCheck: Existing repeated-percentage, throughput, route-cost and finance-adjacent ideas operate different mathematical or technical systems. This record must operate a month-by-month business cash ledger, payment timing, cash-profit distinction and remedy consequences, not percentage growth or generic arithmetic.

syllabusObjectives.claim: why cash is important to a business
what a cash flow forecast is and why it is important
main features of a cash flow forecast: cash inflow, cash outflow, net cash flow, opening balance, closing balance
amend or complete a simple cash flow forecast
interpret a simple cash flow forecast
how a short-term cash flow problem may be overcome: overdraft, delaying supplier payments, asking customers to pay more quickly, delay purchase of non-current assets

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Business 0264 syllabus 2027-2029
references.teachingConnection: Authoritative Section 5.2 outcomes and depth.

references.title: Director information hub: Cashflow
references.teachingConnection: Supports cash timing, payment delays, bill payment and the risk of cash shortage even when a business is trading effectively.
references.locator: Cash-flow and late-payment guidance.

references.title: Preparing for funding applications
references.teachingConnection: The cash-flow forecast section specifies money in, money out, running totals, bank-payment timing, seasonality and contingency room.
references.locator: Section `Prepare a cash flow forecast`.

references.title: Cambridge coursebook rolling cash-flow forecast
references.teachingConnection: The cash-flow cycle, monthly forecasts and remedy table expose the exact running-balance identities and show that payment timing, not invoicing alone, determines available cash.
references.locator: Excerpt PDF pp.2-5 and 8-9 / printed pp.294-297 and 300-301, cash-flow cycle and Tables 24.1-24.3.

transferableMechanism.control: Move a stated receipt or payment to a different month, or apply one syllabus remedy with explicit supplied terms.
transferableMechanism.stateChange: Net cash flow and every later opening and closing balance recalculate on the same retained timeline.
transferableMechanism.feedback: The first shortfall and later balances show whether the timing change or remedy works and support a revised choice.

interaction.learnerAction: Place supplied cash-event cards on a short seeded timeline, calculate and enter the affected totals in the working area, predict the first shortfall, then move one receipt or payment or apply one remedy with explicit terms and revise from the full timeline.
interaction.visibleChange: Checked working populates the persistent timeline; moving an event changes the affected net and closing balances from that month onward, while the first negative balance and any explicit overdraft charge or shifted payment stay visible. The lab checks learner work rather than filling it in.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Cash flow is governed by timing as well as totals: opening balance plus net cash flow produces closing balance, which becomes the next opening balance. A profitable business can still lack cash when receipts arrive after payments are due.
modelLimitations: Use only supplied amounts, dates and remedy terms; do not invent supplier sentiment, customer behaviour, credit limits or business-success scores.
This is a cash-timing model, not a profit forecast or financial recommendation.

records.distinctGap: A persistent month-by-month ledger makes one timing change cascade through every later balance, exposing why cash and profit differ.

assessment.summary: Curriculum importance 2: exact §5.2 covers calculation, amendment, interpretation and remedies. Concept strength 2: one timing change cascades through a persistent ledger. Authentic experimental potential 2: forecast amendment is the syllabus operation. Resource quality 2: coursebook identities and government timing guidance are sufficient foundations. Overlap risk 2: no deployed lab owns this business cash-timing system. Need for interactivity 2: reversible timing and seeded cases materially exceed one worked table. Tier judgment: build-now; rank 15 remains later packet priority.

records.revisedDirection: Use a persistent event timeline, not an auto-completing spreadsheet. Learners place supplied receipts and payments, record the affected calculation in the working area and then see the checked cascade through net, opening and closing cash. Permit only remedies with explicit supplied arithmetic. Exclude hidden risk scores and invented supplier, customer or investment responses.

transferableMechanism.control: Move one consistently quoted exchange rate while fixed foreign-currency import and export invoices remain visible.
transferableMechanism.stateChange: The home-currency import cost and export revenue, or the foreign-currency price needed to preserve home revenue, recalculate together.
transferableMechanism.feedback: The paired importer/exporter view exposes the directional consequence and supports revising a pricing or sourcing explanation.

interaction.learnerAction: Read one explicit quote convention, predict both business effects, then move the rate on a labelled conversion bridge while fixed import and export invoices remain visible; choose what the exporter holds constant and revise the explanation from the paired money flows.
interaction.visibleChange: The same rate movement changes two retained before/after flows: foreign invoice to home-currency import cost, and home export price or revenue to its foreign-currency counterpart. Numeric conversions support the visual relationship rather than becoming the whole activity.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: With a consistent quotation, appreciation makes foreign-currency imports cheaper in home currency but tends to make home exports dearer abroad; depreciation reverses those pressures. The exact business effect depends on which price or revenue is held constant.
modelLimitations: Use one fictional currency pair, explicit invoice amounts and a fixed quote convention; never use live rates or imply a forecast.
Do not simulate demand, competitiveness scores, tariffs, quotas, globalisation or multinational host-country effects.

records.distinctGap: A paired conversion bridge makes one exchange-rate movement produce opposite, inspectable business consequences without becoming a calculator or broad globalisation dashboard.

assessment.summary: Curriculum importance 2: the narrowed concept covers the exact §6.2 exchange-rate outcomes. Concept strength 2: one rate produces a synchronized importer/exporter state. Authentic experimental potential 2: invoice revaluation is a real deterministic business operation. Resource quality 2: syllabus and book diagrams fully ground the direction. Overlap risk 2: the paired exposure is distinct from generic conversion. Need for interactivity 2: rate manipulation and held-constant choices reveal relationships one static case cannot. Tier judgment: build-now; rank 19 remains later packet priority.

records.revisedDirection: Narrow completely to exchange-rate exposure: one explicit quote, fixed invoices and a synchronized visual conversion bridge for importer and exporter. Require a directional prediction before movement and keep the resulting money flows visible. Do not make a currency calculator, and exclude live rates, demand models, tariffs, quotas, MNCs and broad globalisation outcomes.

transferableMechanism.control: Choose a replenishment order for the next period while demand and the delivery queue remain visible.

references.teachingConnection: Tables 21.1-21.2 and the revision mind map contrast end-of-process checking with standards applied through the process, including scrap, rework, complaints and shared responsibility.
references.locator: Excerpt PDF pp.3-5 / printed pp.260-262, Tables 21.1-21.2 and revision mind map.

transferableMechanism.control: Place a stated process standard or an inspection point, then introduce a specified process deviation.
transferableMechanism.stateChange: The same item path shows the deviation corrected during the process, detected only after output, or escaping to the customer.
transferableMechanism.feedback: The visible correction, rework and escape path supports revising the balance of assurance and control.

interaction.learnerAction: Place a small set of stated process standards, in-process checks and output inspections on one visible workflow, introduce a named deviation, predict where it can first be surfaced and choose the corrective response, then revise the arrangement from the trace.
interaction.visibleChange: The item and deviation remain visible as they move through the workflow. A relevant process check flags non-conformance earlier and routes it for corrective action; an output inspection flags it later for rework; an uncovered deviation reaches the customer.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Quality assurance uses planned standards and process checks to reduce the chance of failure and surface causes earlier; quality control inspects output to detect failure. Neither guarantees quality, and late detection creates more rework or customer exposure.
modelLimitations: Use explicit named deviations and deterministic routes; do not invent defect probabilities, hidden quality scores or monetary estimates.
The model explains earlier process assurance versus output detection; it must not imply that assurance automatically corrects a defect or guarantees conforming output.

records.distinctGap: A persistent item-and-deviation trace makes earlier assurance versus later output detection visible without turning quality into an arbitrary score or guarantee.

records.learningGap: Learners may memorise aerobic and anaerobic equations without connecting oxygen availability to pathway choice, products and relative energy release, or may transfer the yeast alcohol/carbon-dioxide pathway to vigorous muscle activity. The 0610 active-transport extension should be a cross-link to the membrane record, not a duplicate transport mode.

interaction.visibleChange: One persistent system tracks the airway route, alveolus-capillary interface, inspired and expired oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour, plus the limewater result. Correct airflow through the paired apparatus makes the expired-air sample turn limewater cloudy sooner. A thin, large, ventilated and well-supplied surface maintains oxygen movement into blood and carbon-dioxide movement out; one altered feature changes the trace, while a missing control or reversed apparatus makes the conclusion uncertain.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The breathing system carries air to alveoli and associated capillaries. Efficient human gas exchange depends on a large, thin surface with good blood supply and ventilation. Oxygen enters blood, carbon dioxide leaves it, and expired air contains less oxygen, more carbon dioxide and more water vapour than inspired air; limewater supplies evidence specifically for carbon dioxide.

interaction.visibleChange: A pressure trace is highest and pulsatile in the artery, falls across the capillary bed and is lower in the vein. An artery wall withstands the incoming pulse, an intact vein valve blocks reversal, and a thin capillary interface lets bounded materials reach or leave nearby cells. interaction.conceptualConclusion: Artery, vein and capillary structures fit different pressures and functions: arteries have relatively thick walls and narrower lumens, veins have relatively thinner walls, wider lumens and valves, and capillary walls provide the short exchange interface. syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe the characteristics of living organisms by defining: (a) movement as an action by an organism or part of an organism causing a change of position or place (b) respiration as the chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules and release energy for metabolism (c) sensitivity as the ability to detect and respond to changes in the internal or external environment (d) growth as a permanent increase in size and dry mass (e) reproduction as the processes that make more of the same kind of organism (f) excretion as the removal of waste products of metabolism and substances in excess of requirements (g) nutrition as the taking in of materials for energy, growth and development

records.overlapCheck: No current record or deployed lab operates household electrical fault and protection decisions. It must remain separate from ordinary low-voltage circuit construction because its safety framing and permissible actions differ.

Explain the use and operation of trip switches and fuses and choose appropriate fuse ratings and trip switch settings (knowledge of RCDs (Residual Current Devices) is not required)
Explain why the outer casing of an electrical appliance must be either non-conducting (double-insulated) or earthed

interaction.learnerAction: Inspect a synthetic appliance scenario, identify conductor and insulation faults, choose switch/fuse/earth protection, then run the case and revise the protection plan.
interaction.visibleChange: The model traces a safe or hazardous current path and shows whether the selected protective device disconnects the supply under the supplied fault current.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Heating rises with current and resistance, switches and fuses belong in the live conductor, and earthing plus correctly rated protection limits fault danger.

records.distinctGap: It exposes the causal path from a fault through current and protection while avoiding real electrical hazards.

assessment.summary: Curriculum importance 2: exact syllabus and book evidence cover wiring, faults and protection. Concept strength 2: fault and protection choices produce an inspectable current path and revisable outcome. Authentic experimental potential 2: appliance-fault diagnosis is authentic while remaining safely synthetic. Resource quality 2: the coursebook, exact OpenStax sequence and HSE guidance collectively support the rules. Overlap risk 2: no deployed lab owns this relationship. Need for interactivity 2: changing one fault/protection state explains functions more clearly than labelling a fixed diagram. Tier judgment: build-now; rank 65 records lower packet priority, not ineligibility.

records.revisedDirection: Use one synthetic appliance and a visible current path. Let a learner change the supplied fault and protection, then inspect danger or disconnection and revise. Translate terminology to Cambridge live/neutral/earth, exclude real-work instructions and avoid a fuse-calculation quiz shell.

records.title: Mass, Weight and Density
records.learningGap: Learners may use mass and weight interchangeably, assume an object’s mass changes on another planet, or calculate density without connecting displacement measurements and relative density to whether an object floats or sinks.
records.overlapCheck: No current science record or deployed lab covers mass-weight distinction, density measurement or float/sink prediction. This remains separate from generic measurement reliability because the object’s physical properties and gravitational field create the consequential state.

records.title: Metal Reactivity and Extraction
records.learningGap: Learners may memorise a reactivity order and separate industrial facts without using reaction evidence to justify the order or using carbon's position to decide why iron and aluminium require different extraction routes. They need a connected inference chain from observations to order, route and process evidence.
records.overlapCheck: Electrolysis and Charge Transfer covers charge flow and electrode products, Physical, Chemical and Redox Changes covers redox definitions, and Giant Structures and Metal Properties covers metallic structure. None uses water/acid/displacement results to infer a metal order and make an ore-extraction decision; no deployed lab covers this relationship.

Resource quality 2: book, OpenStax and WJEC foundations collectively support the complete bounded sequence. Overlap risk 2: no deployed lab owns this mechanism. Describe the advantages and disadvantages of an automated system used for a given scenario

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 126-132

references.title: Online PLC simulator
references.teachingConnection: Conveyor, tank and traffic-light stations show authentic fault and I/O consequences; use as a richness reference only.

references.title: micro:bit Auto-farmer
references.teachingConnection: Grounds sensors, a programmed decision and actuator response in a real automated growing system.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 syllabus, 2026-2028
references.teachingConnection: Sets the component collaboration outcome and permits scenario-linked drawbacks without requiring a wider reliability or robotics unit.

references.title: Automated Systems - CIE IGCSE Computer Science Revision Notes
references.teachingConnection: Lists equipment failure and calibration as scenario-relevant drawbacks, while its worked example makes each stage's contribution explicit.

references.title: Control Systems - Computer Science GCSE GURU
references.teachingConnection: Emphasises that input devices do not make decisions or directly operate outputs, providing a basis for tracing which link is responsible for a wrong result.

interaction.learnerAction: Run one scenario, inject exactly one fault in the sensor, processor rule or actuator, and predict the resulting output before revealing the trace.
interaction.visibleChange: The earliest broken stage is highlighted, the final actuator outcome is shown, and the interface labels the corresponding scenario drawback such as equipment failure or incorrect processing.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A sensor supplies data, a microprocessor makes the decision and an actuator performs the action; a fault at each stage produces a different observable failure signature.

records.revisedDirection: Do not build this candidate. The deployed Automated Systems builder already lets learners construct the sensor → ADC → microprocessor → comparison → decision → actuator loop, run batches, see the earliest failing stage and physical route, receive pass/fail evidence and revise the chart. A separate injected-fault tracer would duplicate that component-role attribution and diagnostic feedback.
records.distinctGap: No standalone gap remains: the deployed Automated Systems builder already attributes observable failures to sensor, conversion, processor/comparison and actuator choices.

assessment.summary: Remove overlap. The live builder already teaches the same diagnosis from synchronized process and outcome evidence, while the claimed PLC/micro:bit sources do not establish an independent fault-injection lab.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Automated System Components Across Scenarios

The distinct gap is structural transfer, not another themed simulation.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe how sensors, microprocessors and actuators can be used in collaboration to create automated systems
Describe the advantages and disadvantages of an automated system used for a given scenario

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 126-132

references.title: micro:bit Auto-farmer
references.teachingConnection: Grounds sensors, a programmed decision and actuator response in a real automated growing system.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 syllabus, 2026-2028

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science - Automated Systems video
references.teachingConnection: Exam-focused explanation introduces sensors, microprocessors and actuators together and frames advantages and disadvantages through varied scenarios.

references.title: 0478 Unit 7: Automated and emerging technologies
references.teachingConnection: A 0478-aligned unit explicitly covers the sensor, microprocessor and actuator collaboration and scenario coverage, supporting a transfer-focused activity.

interaction.learnerAction: Select one of the seven syllabus scenario families and match a supplied sensor reading, microprocessor rule and actuator action into the correct three-stage chain.
interaction.visibleChange: The same three-stage diagram stays in place while its labels and causal trace update for each scenario; an incorrect role placement leaves a visibly broken chain and gives a local explanation.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The architecture transfers across contexts; the measured quantity, decision rule and physical action change, but the sensor -> microprocessor -> actuator roles remain distinct.

records.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.

assessment.summary: Transfer across contexts is valuable, but seven scenario families invite breadth and card-matching repetition. The core causal chain is taught more directly by automation-chain-builder; transfer is better considered after that concept has a proven lab.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Binary and Hexadecimal Place Value
records.learningGap: Learners may perform isolated conversion rules without seeing that denary, binary and hexadecimal are synchronized place-value descriptions of the same integer, or why one hexadecimal digit corresponds exactly to four binary bits.
records.overlapCheck: The committed Binary Number Practice lab is a broad generated question bank covering conversions, arithmetic, signed representations and related notation. It checks fluency but does not let learners construct one value across binary place values, four-bit groups and base-16 place values, so this conceptual lab has a distinct role and should lead into that practice lab rather than replace it.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand how and why computers use binary to represent all forms of data
Understand the denary, binary and hexadecimal number systems
Convert between positive denary and positive binary, positive denary and positive hexadecimal, and positive hexadecimal and positive binary
Understand how and why hexadecimal is used as a beneficial method of data representation
Show understanding of different number systems and convert an integer value from one number base or representation to another

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 10-16

references.title: CS Unplugged: How binary digits work
references.teachingConnection: Its binary cards make powers of two visible: showing or hiding a card changes the represented sum, and the largest-to-smallest subtraction method exposes why each bit becomes 1 or 0.

references.title: University of Chicago: Number systems
references.teachingConnection: The hexadecimal section connects one hex digit to four bits through 16 = 2^4 and shows a denary value becoming grouped binary and then hexadecimal.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Defines the three positive-integer conversion relationships and the reason for hexadecimal at the required depth.

references.title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science 9618 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Confirms the same binary, denary and hexadecimal conversion foundation for AS and A Level learners.

interaction.learnerAction: Construct or alter one positive integer using visible binary place values, then inspect and complete its four-bit grouping and direct base-16 decomposition.
interaction.visibleChange: The active binary sum and remainder, nibble values, hexadecimal symbols and base-16 quotient/remainder update together while retaining one denary identity.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Binary and hexadecimal are place-value representations of the same integer; four binary bits map to one hexadecimal digit because 16 equals 2 to the power of 4, and direct division by 16 reaches the same hexadecimal result.

records.revisedDirection: Build a mathematics-style guided place-value lab around one synchronized integer. Begin with bit places that double and can be included or excluded, expose each four-bit group as one 0-F value, and make denary to binary to hexadecimal visibly converge with direct denary division/decomposition by 16. Preserve reverse reading within the same model, use replayable varied values where reliable, and hand breadth, speed practice, arithmetic and signed representations to Binary Number Practice.
records.distinctGap: No committed live lab makes one integer directly operable across binary place values, four-bit groups and base-16 place values while comparing both denary-to-hexadecimal methods.

assessment.summary: This is a central prerequisite with a verified conceptual gap beside the existing practice bank. Cambridge's place-value treatment and the CS Unplugged binary-card operation support one consequential construction rather than a click-through conversion explanation. Synchronizing the binary construction, four-bit grouping and direct base-16 route makes the equivalence inspectable and gives learners evidence they can use to revise their own representation.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Blockchain Structure and Tamper Evidence
records.learningGap: Learners may repeat that blockchain records cannot be altered without seeing how changing an earlier transaction invalidates the later linked records.
records.overlapCheck: No live blockchain lab exists. Encryption and Parity/ARQ are adjacent but teach confidentiality and transmission-error handling rather than tamper evidence.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the concept of a digital currency and how digital currencies are used
Understand the process of blockchain and how it is used to track digital currency transactions

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 105-106

references.title: MIT Digital Currency Initiative: Blockchain
references.teachingConnection: In the five-block chain, edit Data and inspect Prev, Hash and Nonce: the changed block and every later link turn invalid until the chain is re-mined in order.
references.locator: Five-block chain with editable Data, Prev, Hash, Nonce and Mine controls.

references.title: NISTIR 8202 Blockchain Technology Overview
references.teachingConnection: Section 3.7, Figure 3 and Section 7.1 ground chained block hashes and the precise tamper-evident/resistant claim.

references.title: Bitcoin Developer Guide: Block Chain
references.teachingConnection: Explains how block headers link to previous blocks, grounding the visible broken-link consequence after an earlier record changes.

interaction.learnerAction: Append transactions to a short chain, alter an earlier record, identify the first broken link, then re-mine blocks in the required order and compare the resulting chain evidence.
interaction.visibleChange: The altered block receives a different hash, each later previous-hash link becomes invalid, and repairing one block leaves later links broken until they are rebuilt in sequence.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Linked fingerprints make an earlier change detectable because the following records no longer point to the altered record.

records.revisedDirection: Use one short persistent ledger. Learners append, alter, locate the first invalid link and rebuild in order while a retained before-state exposes the evidence of change. Keep proof-of-work simplified and describe the outcome as tamper-evident/resistant, not magically immutable or a full consensus simulation.
records.distinctGap: Teaches tamper evidence across linked transaction records, not data-transmission error checking, confidentiality or packet routing.

assessment.summary: Build now. The operated MIT chain and NIST Figure 3 directly ground append → alter → downstream invalidation, while ordered repair makes link dependency consequential. No live lab owns tamper evidence; keep the claim precise and do not imply that a simplified local chain is absolutely immutable.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Browser Rendering of HTML
records.learningGap: Learners can confuse a web browser with a search engine or assume the server sends finished pixels, missing that the browser retrieves and renders HTML into the displayed page.
records.overlapCheck: Closest existing labs are software-stack (browser shown as generic application content) and translator (code output, not browser rendering). Neither exposes the browser's retrieve-and-render role for an HTML response.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Explain the purpose and functions of a web browser

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 96-102

references.title: How browsers load websites - MDN
references.teachingConnection: Grounds browser retrieval and rendering responsibilities.

references.title: Browsing the web - MDN
references.teachingConnection: MDN explicitly separates a browser, which retrieves and displays pages, from a search engine, which helps find pages; this supports an original role-identification interaction tied to the rendered result.

interaction.learnerAction: Press Render on a small returned HTML document, then change one tag such as a heading or link before rendering it again.
interaction.visibleChange: The raw response panel stays text while the browser panel changes from plain markup to the corresponding displayed heading, paragraph or link; a search-engine label does not render the document.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The browser is the client software that retrieves web resources and interprets HTML to display a page; it is not the web server or the search service.

records.revisedDirection: Let learners alter a returned HTML document and operate a browser whose rendered result changes while the raw response remains inspectable.
records.distinctGap: It teaches the browser's interpretation of returned HTML, not translator execution or generic software-layer placement.

assessment.summary: Editing one tag and seeing rendered output is legible, but it may collapse into a miniature HTML editor and does not by itself resolve the browser-versus-search-engine misconception. The retrieved-to-rendered transition needs stronger instructional framing.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Web Browser Functions
records.learningGap: The syllabus names address bar, navigation, tabs, history, bookmarks and cookie storage, but learners may conflate these browser functions with a web page or search engine.
records.overlapCheck: Closest existing lab is software-stack, which only includes a generic browser application tile. No existing lab makes browser functions consequential, though this idea overlaps conceptually with the browser-rendering and cookie candidates above.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Explain the purpose and functions of a web browser

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 96-102

references.title: MDN: how browsers load websites
references.teachingConnection: Grounds browser retrieval and rendering responsibilities.

references.title: Browsing the web - MDN
references.teachingConnection: MDN frames the browser as software that retrieves and displays pages and contrasts it with a search engine, giving a reliable role boundary for any browser-function activity.

references.title: Tips & Shortcuts for Better Browsing - Chrome
references.teachingConnection: The Chrome reference demonstrates concrete browser functions such as tabs, bookmarks, history and reopening pages; it can supply scenario vocabulary while the lab remains an original, minimal interaction.

interaction.learnerAction: Choose one browser function for each short scenario, such as returning to a page, keeping two pages open or entering a page address.
interaction.visibleChange: The selected browser control performs the scenario in a small mock browser, while choosing a search-engine or page action produces a local explanation of the role mismatch.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A web browser is software with several navigation, retrieval, display and storage functions; a web page and a search engine are different things.

records.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
records.distinctGap: It surveys browser functions absent from existing labs, but breadth rather than a distinct causal gap currently defines the idea.

assessment.summary: The named functions are syllabus-valid, but matching controls to scenarios is mainly vocabulary recall. Combining tabs, history, bookmarks, navigation, address input and cookies also lacks one teachable centre.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Buffering and Data-Rate Mismatch
records.learningGap: Learners may know that a buffer stores data without understanding how it absorbs a temporary speed mismatch and why it can still overflow.
records.overlapCheck: Memory Management owns RAM/cache/page movement, while Data Transmission Methods and Packet Switching own channel choice, routing and packet travel. This concept must stay at one producer-consumer boundary and operate only rate mismatch, finite occupancy, overflow/backpressure and underrun.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Show understanding of the use of buffers

book.label: AS & A Level coursebook, printed pp. 26-42

references.title: BBC R&D WHP237 Network Behaviour
references.teachingConnection: Section 3.3, Figures 3.3.1–3.3.3 show arrivals faster than an outgoing link filling finite buffers, followed by pause/backpressure or packet drop.
references.locator: §3.3, Figures 3.3.1-3.3.3, printed pp.12-13.

references.title: BBC R&D WHP420 Segmented Media Player Model
references.teachingConnection: Section 5, Figure 7 and Section 9 show occupancy stepping up on arrivals, draining during playback and causing interruption at underrun.
references.locator: §5 Figure 7, printed pp.14-16; §9, printed pp.24-25.

references.title: Cambridge 9618 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Anchors the device-speed mismatch and buffer-purpose outcome.

interaction.learnerAction: Shape a short producer burst, consumer rate and finite capacity, predict whether the buffer will absorb the mismatch, then revise one condition after an overflow or underrun.
interaction.visibleChange: Packets and an occupancy trace fill while arrivals exceed consumption and drain when the consumer catches up; full capacity causes drop/pause and an empty media buffer causes interruption.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A buffer smooths temporary speed differences but finite capacity cannot absorb an indefinite mismatch.

records.revisedDirection: Use one recognisable producer-consumer stream with packets and an occupancy trace. Let rate, burst duration or capacity change the same retained state, then expose overflow, backpressure or underrun. Exclude routing, topology, channel selection and transmission faults as well as fixed animation, generic dashboards and wall-clock performance claims.
records.distinctGap: The adjacent memory and transmission labs do not expose the changing occupancy of one finite I/O buffer between a producer and consumer.

assessment.summary: Build now. Two BBC R&D foundations make finite occupancy, rate mismatch, pause/drop and underrun visible in authentic network/media systems. Learner-shaped bursts and capacity create persistent causal state and a revision loop that a worked rate table cannot preserve; Memory Management covers a different mechanism.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: ASCII and Unicode Character Encoding
records.learningGap: Learners may treat ASCII and Unicode as interchangeable labels without seeing representable-character and storage consequences.
records.overlapCheck: No live lab teaches character sets directly. Binary Number Practice and Bitmap Compression are adjacent data-representation experiences, so a future concept must add a genuinely distinct representability relationship rather than another conversion or storage calculator.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand how and why a computer represents text and the use of character sets, including American standard code for information interchange (ASCII) and Unicode

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 21-23

references.title: Unicode Standard Chapter 2
references.teachingConnection: Section 2.5.3, Table 3-6 and Figure 2-11 show code point to byte sequence and why UTF-8 preserves ASCII characters while wider ranges use more bytes.
references.locator: §2.5.3, Table 3-6 and Figure 2-11.

references.title: Character encodings: Essential concepts
references.teachingConnection: The Character encoding diagram and comparison table separate glyph, character/code point and stored bytes for the same text.
references.locator: Character-encoding diagram and encoding-comparison table.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Computer Science 0478 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Defines the precise ASCII and Unicode learning boundary for an original representation comparison.

interaction.learnerAction: Compose a short string from ASCII and non-ASCII characters, predict which symbols survive a restricted character set, then inspect the character codes and stored bytes before revising the representation.
interaction.visibleChange: Each glyph remains linked to its character/code point and byte sequence; the restricted set exposes an unsupported character while Unicode preserves it, and storage changes remain visible.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A character set maps symbols to codes; a wider repertoire can represent more symbols but affects storage.

records.revisedDirection: Use one editable text surface that keeps glyphs, character codes and bytes linked. Let a restricted ASCII representation fail visibly on a non-ASCII symbol while Unicode preserves it. Stay at Cambridge depth: do not turn the lab into a Unicode-standard tutorial or a byte calculator.
records.distinctGap: Binary Numbers operates numeric place value and Bitmap Compression operates pixel data; this concept uniquely keeps each glyph linked through character/code point to its encoded bytes and exposes unsupported symbols.

assessment.summary: Build now. Exact syllabus/book treatment plus Unicode and W3C visuals ground the character → code → bytes relationship. Learner-authored mixed text creates a consequential representability and storage comparison distinct from numeric conversion, with visible evidence for revision rather than a fixed decoding exercise.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Client–Server and Peer-to-Peer Networks
records.learningGap: Learners may define client-server and peer-to-peer networks without predicting how a failed or unavailable node affects access.
records.overlapCheck: Network Topology models physical/logical connectivity and packet movement, so a network architecture lab is adjacent and needs a distinct service-ownership focus.

references.title: NetLab packet-path simulator
references.teachingConnection: Shows a bounded DNS/ARP/TCP/TLS journey through inspectable network steps.

references.title: NetSim
references.teachingConnection: A rich network-workbench benchmark with devices, commands and packet traces.

references.title: Cambridge 9618 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Defines the network-model comparison without requiring another routing simulator.

interaction.visibleChange: Available copies and requesting nodes update according to where the service resides.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Client-server centralises service provision, while peers can both request and provide resources.

records.distinctGap: Network Topology models physical/logical connectivity and packet movement, so a network architecture lab is adjacent and needs a distinct service-ownership focus.

assessment.summary: promising - One service and one node failure can expose the distinction, but overlap risk requires review. Network Topology models physical/logical connectivity and packet movement, so a network architecture lab is adjacent and needs a distinct service-ownership focus.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Compiler and Interpreter Translation
records.learningGap: Learners may list compiler and interpreter differences without seeing when translation and error discovery happen.
records.overlapCheck: Translator already compares Cambridge pseudocode and Python execution, making a new translation-mode lab adjacent.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Show understanding of how an interpreter executes a high-level language program
Show understanding of the purpose of a compiler
Explain the difference between compilation and interpretation

book.label: AS & A Level coursebook, printed pp. 121-132

references.title: Cambridge 9618 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Defines the timing and diagnostic differences that would have to remain distinct from the Translator lab.

interaction.learnerAction: Run the same fixed three-line program through compile-all and interpret-line routes with an error on line two.
interaction.visibleChange: The compile route reports before execution while the interpreter executes line one and then stops at line two.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A compiler translates a whole program before execution; an interpreter translates and executes incrementally.

records.revisedDirection: Do not build this candidate. It duplicates an existing or already accepted experience.
records.distinctGap: Translator already compares Cambridge pseudocode and Python execution, making a new translation-mode lab adjacent.

assessment.summary: promising but adjacent - Retain for review rather than duplicate Translator. Translator already compares Cambridge pseudocode and Python execution, making a new translation-mode lab adjacent.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Cookies and Browser State
records.learningGap: Learners may describe cookies as files or tracking alone without seeing how a small browser-stored value is returned with later requests, or how session and persistent lifetimes differ.
records.overlapCheck: Closest existing lab is memory-management, where a browser is only a workload; software-stack has no cookie state. Neither shows a server response changing because a cookie returns with a later request.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Explain what is meant by cookies and how they are used, including session cookies and persistent cookies

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 103-104

references.title: Using HTTP cookies - MDN
references.teachingConnection: Accurate reference for cookie state, expiry and requests.

references.title: What are cookies? - Cloudflare
references.teachingConnection: Cloudflare clearly distinguishes session cookies, which end with a session, from persistent cookies, which carry an expiry, and gives preference, cart and authentication examples matching the syllabus notes.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 2023-25 - Cookies, Session and Persistent - YouTube
references.teachingConnection: This syllabus-focused lesson explicitly covers cookies and the session/persistent distinction, providing a learner-language reference and coverage check without importing its presentation.

interaction.learnerAction: Sign in to a fictional site, open a second page, then choose whether the site stores the state as a session cookie or a persistent cookie before closing and reopening the browser.
interaction.visibleChange: The second request shows the cookie being sent and receives a personalized page; after restart the session version disappears while the persistent version still changes the server response.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A cookie is small browser-stored data that a server can use to recognize a later request; session cookies end with the session, while persistent cookies survive until their expiry.

records.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
records.distinctGap: It teaches browser-held web state persisting across requests and optionally across restart, unlike Memory Management's page/cache movement or Software Stack's component dependencies.

assessment.summary: The current browser experience coherently exposes state across requests and restarts, but the topic is not complex enough to justify further automated polish or rollout ahead of stronger conceptual candidates. Preserve it for later human review.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Digital Signatures and Message Integrity
records.learningGap: Learners may confuse encryption for confidentiality with a digital signature that proves origin and detects alteration.
records.overlapCheck: The live Encryption in Data Transmission lab teaches confidentiality and public/private key roles. This concept must keep the message readable throughout and operate origin/authenticity and alteration detection, never repeat the watched-channel secrecy surface.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Show understanding of digital certification

book.label: A Level coursebook, printed pp. 386-396

references.title: NIST Digital Signature Standard
references.teachingConnection: Figure 1 and Figures 3–4 show message hashing, private-key signing and public-key verification ending in valid or invalid.

references.title: Digital Signature Demo
references.teachingConnection: Generate a key pair, sign and verify an editable message; changing one character makes verification fail while the message remains readable.
references.locator: Generate key pair, Sign and Verify workflow.

references.title: Cambridge 9618 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Defines signature authentication and integrity as distinct from confidentiality.

interaction.learnerAction: Sign a readable message with the named sender's private key, verify it with the corresponding public key, then alter the message or claimed signer and diagnose the failed verification.
interaction.visibleChange: The message stays readable while its digest/signature path ends valid only for the unchanged message and matching public key; alteration or the wrong signer produces a visible mismatch.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A digital signature does not hide a message; it provides evidence of origin and detects a change.

records.revisedDirection: Use one readable message and a compact signature path. Let content or signer evidence change and make verification fail at the digest/public-key comparison. Keep confidentiality, blockchain, certificate infrastructure and cryptographic mathematics outside the central interaction.
records.distinctGap: The deployed encryption lab teaches message confidentiality and key roles; a signature lab remains distinct only if origin/authenticity verification—not secrecy—is the operated consequence.

assessment.summary: Build now. NIST's paired signing/verification diagrams and the operated Heron demo ground the private-sign/public-verify relationship and exact-message integrity. Altering content or signer creates consequential evidence distinct from the deployed encryption lab's confidentiality outcome.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: DNS and Web Page Retrieval
records.learningGap: Learners often memorize browser, DNS, IP, server and HTML as a list without seeing why the browser must resolve a domain before it can request and display a page.
records.overlapCheck: Closest existing labs are network-topology (generic packet routing) and software-stack (generic browser app). Neither models the distinct web retrieval chain from URL through DNS/IP and web server to returned HTML.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe how web pages are located, retrieved and displayed on a device when a user enters a URL

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 96-102

references.title: NetLab packet-path simulator
references.teachingConnection: Shows a bounded DNS/ARP/TCP/TLS journey through inspectable network steps.

references.title: How the web works - MDN
references.teachingConnection: Grounds the request sequence without prescribing a lab shell.

references.title: Populating the page: how browsers work - MDN
references.teachingConnection: The article anchors navigation at URL entry, then separates DNS lookup, connection, HTTP GET, HTML response and rendering; the lab should stop at the syllabus level instead of reproducing its deeper performance detail.

references.title: How DNS Works - Interactive Visualization
references.teachingConnection: Exposes resolver, root, TLD, authoritative and cache state.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 0478 | Internet & WWW - YouTube
references.teachingConnection: The syllabus-specific video explicitly includes how web pages are requested and retrieved, providing a direct teaching coverage reference and vocabulary check; no media or presentation should be reused.

interaction.learnerAction: Enter one fictional URL and advance the request one stage at a time: browser parses it, DNS supplies an IP address, the browser requests the server, the server returns HTML, and the browser displays it.
interaction.visibleChange: One highlighted message moves through five quiet panels; each stage fills its result, and a wrong DNS mapping visibly prevents the request reaching the intended server until corrected.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A human-readable URL does not directly reach a page: DNS maps its domain to an IP address, HTTP retrieves HTML from the web server, and the browser renders that HTML for the user.

records.revisedDirection: Make the browser the instrument: diagnose a convincing wrong/no-page result, inspect compact DNS-IP-request-HTML evidence, repair the mapping and rerun.
records.distinctGap: It teaches ordered URL resolution and page retrieval; Network Topology only models generic packet movement and Software Stack only shows a generic browser layer.

assessment.summary: This directly answers a multi-role syllabus outcome through a single request whose dependency chain is visible. A deliberately wrong DNS mapping creates a meaningful failure and correction, while five fixed stages cap the scope.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Encryption in Data Transmission
records.learningGap: Learners can repeat that encryption keeps data safe but may not connect that claim to the observable difference between plaintext and ciphertext on a shared transmission path, or to the exact key action that lets the intended receiver recover the message.
records.overlapCheck: The current catalogue has no encryption lab. Parity & ARQ models transmission errors and retries, while Network Topology and CSMA/CD model routing or contention; none hide message content or teach symmetric/asymmetric key use. The three immutable reference labs also contain no encryption interaction.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 49-51

references.title: OpenLearn: the key distribution problem
references.teachingConnection: Frames the practical problem of sharing a symmetric secret over a watched channel.

references.title: Public Key Cryptography Interactivity | NRICH
references.teachingConnection: Makes Alice, Bob, Eve and key-role consequences concrete.

references.title: Public Key Cryptography - Computerphile
references.teachingConnection: The Computerphile video explains public/private key cryptography through a concrete communication analogy. It is useful inspiration for a visually legible message journey and role separation, not for reproducing its media or implementation.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 0478/11 Paper 1 May/Jun 2024
references.teachingConnection: The official paper asks learners to place plain text, cipher text, public key, and private key in an asymmetric-transmission sequence. This anchors the interaction vocabulary and intended exam-level outcome.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner sends a short message through a channel after choosing either no encryption, a shared symmetric key, or the receiver's public/private key route.
interaction.visibleChange: An eavesdropper panel shows readable plaintext on the open route, ciphertext on encrypted routes, and whether the receiver can recover the message with the selected key; a wrong key leaves the message locked.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Encryption protects data in transit by transforming plaintext into ciphertext. Symmetric encryption uses the same secret key at both ends, while asymmetric encryption uses the receiver's public key to encrypt and private key to decrypt.

records.revisedDirection: One secure-communications workbench: operate key chips, encryptor/decryptor sockets, a watched link and retained captured traffic. Shared-key handoff and public/private roles belong inside this one system.
records.distinctGap: It teaches confidentiality and endpoint key actions; Parity/ARQ teaches corrupted-frame detection and retransmission, while the network labs teach movement and contention.

assessment.summary: The syllabus outcome, official assessment vocabulary, NRICH role model and Computerphile explanation converge on one inspectable transmission. The learner can compare readable plaintext, ciphertext and successful key use without implementing cryptographic mathematics or a network simulator.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Data Error Detection Methods
records.learningGap: Learners may confuse parity, checksum, echo check and check digit purposes.
records.overlapCheck: Parity & ARQ already teaches parity detection and retransmission, so automation would substantially duplicate an existing lab.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need to check for errors after data transmission and how these errors can occur
Describe the processes involved in each of the following error detection methods for detecting errors in data after transmission: parity check (odd and even), checksum and echo check
Describe how a check digit is used to detect errors in data entry and identify examples of when a check digit is used, including international standard book numbers (ISBN) and bar codes
Describe how an automatic repeat query (ARQ) can be used to establish that data is received without error

references.title: Hamming code playground
