references.title: Cambridge Resource Plus 0478 Data Transmission
references.teachingConnection: Provides syllabus-aligned error-checking contexts but overlaps the existing Parity & ARQ realization.

interaction.learnerAction: Match a small set of transmission scenarios to the check method that can expose the stated error.
interaction.visibleChange: A fixed payload shows what each selected method can and cannot detect.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Different checking methods add different evidence and do not all detect or correct the same faults.

records.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
records.distinctGap: Parity & ARQ already teaches parity detection and retransmission, so automation would substantially duplicate an existing lab.

assessment.summary: promising but overlapping - Retain for review only unless narrowed to uncovered method selection. Parity & ARQ already teaches parity detection and retransmission, so automation would substantially duplicate an existing lab.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Expert System Inference
records.learningGap: Learners can name expert-system components without tracing how observations match a rule and produce a recommendation.
records.overlapCheck: The committed Single-Neuron Threshold concept operates weighted activation and a numeric decision boundary. This concept must stay with explicit facts, rules, an agenda and a retained explanation chain rather than become another classifier or general AI surface.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand what is meant by artificial intelligence (AI)
Describe the main characteristics of AI as the collection of data and the rules for using that data, the ability to reason, and it can include the ability to learn and adapt
Explain the basic operation and components of AI systems to simulate intelligent behaviour

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 139-142

references.title: CLIPS User's Guide
references.teachingConnection: Chapters 1–2 and the agenda/watch facts/watch activations commands show facts matching rules, activations entering an agenda, firing and asserting new facts.
references.locator: Ch.1 pp.5-6; Ch.2 pp.22-25 and 45-46; agenda, watch facts and watch activations.

references.title: Forward and Backward Chaining Visualizer
references.teachingConnection: The described Fact A → rule → derived fact → goal chain supports facts/rules/goal highlighting; the separate launch page was inaccessible, so live controls remain unverified.

references.title: Expert Systems
references.teachingConnection: Shows the component sequence and rule-based decision process at the syllabus level.

references.title: VisiRule demos
references.teachingConnection: Shows rule-based decisions and inspectable reasoning paths.

interaction.learnerAction: Build or edit a small rule base, add observations to working memory, predict the next matching rule, then revise a fact or rule after inspecting the inference trace.
interaction.visibleChange: Facts make rules eligible on a visible agenda; firing one asserts a new fact that can activate later rules, and the final recommendation retains its complete reason chain.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: An expert system derives a recommendation by matching supplied facts against rules in its knowledge base through an inference engine.

records.revisedDirection: Use one compact facts/rules/agenda surface. Let learners edit a bounded rule or observation, predict the next activation and use the retained reason chain to repair an incorrect recommendation. Exclude backward chaining, salience conflicts and general AI scope unless required by the selected syllabus depth.
records.distinctGap: Automation Chain Builder concerns sensor-to-actuator control and Single-Neuron Threshold concerns weighted classification; neither operates knowledge-base rules, agenda matching or an explained recommendation chain.

assessment.summary: Build now. The CLIPS trace directly grounds facts → matching activation → rule firing → derived fact, while learner-authored facts/rules turn the experience into a small knowledge-engineering system rather than a step revealer. The retained reason chain is distinct from automated control flow.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: File Organisation and Hash-Based Access
records.learningGap: Learners may conflate file organisation with access method and assume hashing always reaches a record in one step.
records.overlapCheck: No matching live lab exists; the archived staged candidate is not deployment evidence. The book’s collision explanation and worked question remain the strongest current treatment.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Show understanding of the methods of file organisation and select an appropriate method of file organisation and file access for a given problem
Show understanding of methods of file access
Show understanding of hashing algorithms

book.label: A Level coursebook, printed pp. 313-327

references.title: VisuAlgo Hash Table
references.teachingConnection: Animated Search, Insert and Remove operations expose home addresses, many-to-one collisions and chaining or probing paths.
references.locator: Hash Table overview and animated Search, Insert and Remove sections.

references.title: File Access
references.teachingConnection: The Types of File Access matrix and examples distinguish sequential scanning, direct access and hashing from key to address.

interaction.learnerAction: Insert and retrieve learner-chosen record keys in one visible store, predict each home address, then resolve a collision and compare the resulting lookup path with a sequential scan.
interaction.visibleChange: The hash calculation points to an address; a collision opens a visible chain or probe path, and later retrieval follows that retained structure while the sequential comparison highlights every inspected record.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Organisation and access are separate choices; hashing maps keys to addresses, but collisions require an additional resolution step.

records.revisedDirection: Use one visible record store. Let learner-chosen keys determine home addresses, retain collisions and make later lookup follow the constructed chain/probe path; compare only with a short sequential scan. Avoid four disconnected route buttons or filesystem implementation detail.
records.distinctGap: No current lab teaches serial, sequential or random file organisation, direct access, record keys or hash collisions; Memory Management is unrelated storage movement.

assessment.summary: Build now. VisuAlgo directly operates insertion, search and collision resolution, while the Cambridge-aligned access matrix grounds the file-access comparison. Learner-chosen keys create a persistent store and genuine collision/retrieval consequences that materially exceed a worked collision.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: File Processing and Exception Handling
records.learningGap: Learners may add exception syntax mechanically without understanding which state must be preserved when a file operation fails.
records.overlapCheck: Translator executes programs but does not focus on file state or exception recovery; this may still be better as a coding exercise than a conceptual lab.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Write code to perform file-processing operations
Show understanding of an exception and the importance of exception handling
Know when it is appropriate to use exception handling
Write program code to use exception handling

book.label: A Level coursebook, printed pp. 443-458

references.title: Cambridge 9618 syllabus
references.teachingConnection: Defines the file and exception outcome and supports keeping the concept to one failed operation.

interaction.learnerAction: Run one fixed file read with a missing record, then choose the recovery action.
interaction.visibleChange: The unhandled route stops with partial state while the handled route closes the file and produces a controlled result.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Exception handling separates an anticipated failure path from the normal path and preserves controlled program state.

records.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
records.distinctGap: Translator executes programs but does not focus on file state or exception recovery; this may still be better as a coding exercise than a conceptual lab.

assessment.summary: uncertain - Bounded but weak fit for the visual lab catalogue. Translator executes programs but does not focus on file state or exception recovery; this may still be better as a coding exercise than a conceptual lab.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Binary Floating-Point Precision and Range
records.learningGap: Learners may normalise a single value procedurally without understanding how mantissa and exponent allocation constrain precision and range.
records.overlapCheck: Binary Numbers does not teach floating-point normalisation, rounding, underflow or overflow.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe the format of binary floating-point real numbers
Understand of the effects of changing the allocation of bits to mantissa and exponent in a floating-point representation
Normalise floating-point numbers
Show understanding of the consequences of a binary representation only being an approximation to the real number it represents (in certain cases)
Understand how underflow and overflow can occur
Show understanding that binary representations can give rise to rounding errors

book.label: A Level coursebook, printed pp. 313-327

references.title: University of Illinois Floating-Point Systems
references.teachingConnection: Lets a fixed floating-point system expose representable values, precision and range.

interaction.learnerAction: Allocate a fixed small bit budget between mantissa and exponent, then try to represent one precise and one very large value.
interaction.visibleChange: A number line shows representable steps, rounding and any underflow or overflow as the allocation changes.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: More mantissa bits improve precision while more exponent bits extend range; a fixed representation cannot maximise both.

records.revisedDirection: Give a concrete measurement task a fixed bit budget; reallocate mantissa/exponent bits and inspect number-line gaps, rounding, underflow and overflow.
records.distinctGap: Binary Numbers does not teach floating-point normalisation, rounding, underflow or overflow.

assessment.summary: Buildable and now implemented. The committed lab fixes the representation rules and makes the mantissa/exponent allocation trade-off visible without becoming an IEEE-754 calculator. Binary Numbers does not teach floating-point normalisation, rounding, underflow or overflow.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Dijkstra’s and A* Search Frontiers
records.learningGap: Learners may execute Dijkstra and A* mechanically without seeing how cost-so-far and a goal-directed heuristic change frontier ordering and exploration.
records.overlapCheck: Network Topology constructs networks and moves packets, but does not teach weighted graph search, frontiers, path costs or heuristics. This must remain an abstract graph rather than a network simulator.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Show understanding of how graphs can be used to aid Artificial Intelligence (AI)

book.label: A Level coursebook, printed pp. 397-410

references.title: VisuAlgo
references.teachingConnection: Learner-supplied data drives structures, algorithms and traces.

references.title: Red Blob Games: Introduction to A*
references.teachingConnection: Excellent frontier, cost and route visibility with meaningful experimentation.

references.title: Amit Patel's A* Pages
references.teachingConnection: Reinforces the weighted graph abstraction, frontier behaviour and pathfinding trade-offs without prescribing a copied design.

interaction.learnerAction: Step Dijkstra and A* across the same fixed eight-node weighted graph, then change one edge weight or destination and rerun.
interaction.visibleChange: Visited nodes, frontier entries and g, h and f values update while the final path and explored-node count remain side by side.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Dijkstra prioritises cost from the start; A* combines that cost with an estimate toward the goal and can explore fewer nodes with a suitable heuristic.

records.revisedDirection: Retain as reference calibration; do not recreate. Its learner-operated frontier, visible g/h/f values and mutable road cost establish the right relationship.
records.distinctGap: Teaches weighted graph search and how a heuristic changes frontier exploration, not network topology or packet movement.

assessment.summary: Highest conceptual leverage and visual fit: Red Blob Games provides an exceptional teaching reference, the Network Topology reference supplies an established SVG language, and the fixed graph keeps scope bounded.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: HTTP and HTTPS Data Transfer
records.learningGap: Learners may treat HTTPS as a different kind of web content or only associate it with a padlock, rather than understanding that it protects ordinary HTTP requests and responses during transfer.
records.overlapCheck: Direct live overlap is now verified: Encryption in Data Transmission owns plaintext-versus-protected transit and observer readability. DNS/Web Page Retrieval owns the browser-to-server retrieval sequence. A separate HTTP/HTTPS lab would repeat the existing causal surface.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe the purpose and operation of hypertext transfer protocol (HTTP) and hypertext transfer protocol secure (HTTPS)

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 96-102

references.title: NetLab packet-path simulator
references.teachingConnection: Shows a bounded DNS/ARP/TCP/TLS journey through inspectable network steps.

references.title: Why is HTTP not secure? HTTP vs. HTTPS - Cloudflare
references.teachingConnection: Cloudflare contrasts plaintext HTTP requests and responses with HTTPS, which uses TLS to encrypt and digitally sign the same HTTP exchange; this supports a restrained observer view of one message rather than a cryptography lesson.

references.title: Overview of HTTP - MDN
references.teachingConnection: MDN defines HTTP as a client-server protocol for fetching resources such as HTML and distinguishes requests from responses, giving the lab its common message shape before the security comparison.

references.title: HTTP vs HTTPS Explained - YouTube
references.teachingConnection: The teaching video presents HTTP and HTTPS through requests, which is a useful reference for learner-facing framing; it is not a source for copied visuals, narration or code.

interaction.learnerAction: Choose HTTP or HTTPS and send the same short fictional GET request containing a harmless example preference to a web server.
interaction.visibleChange: The server receives the same request path in both cases, but an observer panel can read the HTTP payload and sees only an unreadable protected message for HTTPS.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: HTTP carries web requests and responses; HTTPS is the protected form that uses encryption and verification so the exchanged data is not exposed in transit.

records.revisedDirection: Do not build a standalone observer comparison. The deployed Encryption in Data Transmission lab already compares readable and protected traffic on a watched link, including retained captures and key consequences. HTTP request/response framing may be added only as a bounded context or extension there, while DNS/Web Page Retrieval owns the wider browser-request sequence.
records.distinctGap: No standalone gap remains: protected-versus-readable transit is already live in Encryption in Data Transmission, while HTTP framing can be a bounded context there.

assessment.summary: Consolidate. The exact HTTP framing is useful context, but the proposed observer consequence is already live in the encryption workbench and the external sources were not directly inspected. No standalone packet.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Hybrid Symmetric and Asymmetric Encryption
records.learningGap: Learners may see symmetric and asymmetric encryption as competing alternatives and miss the useful division in which asymmetric encryption protects a small shared key while symmetric encryption handles the message itself.
records.overlapCheck: No catalogue lab combines two encryption abstractions, and no current lab covers key setup. This is distinct from the basic public/private route but extends beyond the literal 0478 wording, so it must not become a TLS, certificate, or performance simulation.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 49-51

references.title: OpenLearn: the key distribution problem
references.teachingConnection: Frames the practical problem of sharing a symmetric secret over a watched channel.

references.title: Teach teens computing: Encryption and cryptography | Raspberry Pi Foundation
references.teachingConnection: The Raspberry Pi Foundation course targets ages 14-16, compares symmetric and asymmetric schemes, and explicitly includes a module on the two working together. That provides a concrete teaching reference while the proposed lab uses an original two-envelope abstraction.

references.title: 0478 Unit 2: Data transmission and encryption | PG Online
references.teachingConnection: This 0478-specific unit isolates encryption as its final lesson and states that learners demonstrate both asymmetric and symmetric encryption. It supports curriculum fit, but does not justify adding a broad protocol or HTTPS simulator.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner sends a long message by choosing whether to wrap a short symmetric session key with the receiver's public key before using that session key for the message.
interaction.visibleChange: The channel shows a small protected key envelope followed by one consistent symmetric ciphertext stream; removing the envelope leaves the receiver without the key, while Eve still sees only ciphertext.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The two methods can serve different roles: asymmetric public/private encryption protects key delivery, and symmetric encryption uses the shared key to protect the larger transmitted message.

records.revisedDirection: The curriculum concept may support a worthwhile lab, but the current interaction hypothesis still needs a stronger causal centre before automation.
records.distinctGap: It teaches complementary roles for asymmetric key delivery and symmetric message protection, absent from the current catalogue.

assessment.summary: The envelope model is concrete and well referenced, but the combined modern scheme and implied performance rationale extend beyond the literal 0478 outcome. It risks adding a second cryptographic mechanism before the core distinction is secure.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Logic Circuit Signal Tracing
records.learningGap: Learners may complete isolated truth tables but lose track of intermediate values through a multi-gate circuit.
records.overlapCheck: Absorbed by logic-circuit-builder, which now covers both 0478 and 9618 through construction challenges, live signal tracing, expressions, truth tables, and open experimentation.

Write a logic expression from a: problem statement; logic circuit; truth table

interaction.visibleChange: Each wire lights in sequence and the corresponding truth-table row fills with intermediate and final values.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A compound circuit is evaluated gate by gate, with each output becoming the next gate's input.

records.revisedDirection: The outcome is useful, but a separate package would fragment or duplicate a stronger neighbouring experience. Treat it as a phase, condition or shared cross-curriculum lab.
records.distinctGap: No remaining distinct gap after the cross-syllabus Logic Circuit Builder iteration.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Internet and World Wide Web
records.learningGap: Learners often use Internet and World Wide Web interchangeably, so the dependency between Internet infrastructure and the Web service remains an abstract definition.
records.overlapCheck: Closest existing labs are network-topology (packet movement through a network) and software-stack (a generic browser application tile). Neither distinguishes Internet infrastructure from the Web's browser, HTTP and HTML service.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the difference between the internet and the world wide web

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 96-102

references.title: MDN: how the web works
references.teachingConnection: Grounds the request sequence without prescribing a lab shell.

references.title: World Wide Web - MDN Glossary

references.title: How does the Internet work? - MDN
references.teachingConnection: The article contrasts the Internet as technical infrastructure with the Web as a service and notes that email is another service, giving a concrete non-Web comparison for a restrained classification task.

references.title: IGCSE Computer Science 0478 | Internet & WWW - YouTube
references.teachingConnection: The syllabus-focused lesson covers Internet versus WWW alongside browser, URL and retrieval terms; it is useful as a coverage check, not as a visual or script source.

interaction.learnerAction: Place cards for Internet infrastructure, browser, HTTP, HTML page and email into an Internet layer and a Web-service layer, then remove the Internet layer.
interaction.visibleChange: The Web page lane stops when its infrastructure layer is removed, while the email service remains labelled as a different Internet service; misplaced cards receive local feedback.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: The Internet is the underlying infrastructure; the World Wide Web is one service of linked pages and protocols that uses that infrastructure.

records.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
records.distinctGap: It separates infrastructure from one service, whereas Network Topology teaches packet movement and Software Stack only depicts a browser application.

assessment.summary: The misconception is syllabus-relevant, but the proposed card placement and layer removal remain close to a terminology sort. The email contrast helps, yet the visible consequence is largely definitional rather than an independently explorable mechanism.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Interrupt Handling and ISR Execution
records.learningGap: Learners may know the term interrupt but not the observable sequence in which normal execution pauses, an ISR handles the event, and the original task resumes.
records.overlapCheck: Fetch/Decode/Execute and Assembly show normal instruction execution; neither models an asynchronous event diverting control to an ISR and then returning.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Describe the role and operation of interrupts

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 84-85

references.title: Interrupts, Polling and Handshaking
references.teachingConnection: Provides a clear visual explanation of interrupt-driven control flow suitable as inspiration for a bounded pause-handle-resume trace.

references.title: Computation Structures: Interrupts
references.teachingConnection: Grounds the transfer of control to a handler and return to interrupted computation.

interaction.learnerAction: Step a short foreground task, trigger one keyboard interrupt, step through the ISR, and return to the saved task position.
interaction.visibleChange: A control marker moves from running task to interrupt request to ISR and back to the precise suspended instruction.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: An interrupt temporarily diverts the processor to an ISR; after handling the event, execution resumes rather than restarting.

records.revisedDirection: Do not build this candidate. It duplicates an existing or already accepted experience.
records.distinctGap: Fetch/Decode/Execute and Assembly show normal instruction execution; neither models an asynchronous event diverting control to an ISR and then returning.

assessment.summary: A single asynchronous keyboard event creates a visible pause, handler transfer and exact resume point. The teaching video and university course material ground that control-flow sequence, while fixed foreground and ISR steps prevent expansion into processor architecture.

Construct a logic expression

assessment.summary: worth building - Changing statement placement creates a clear counterfactual: output order changes while call path and peak depth remain invariant. Translator traces programs but does not make retained recursive frames the operated relationship.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Small-Key RSA and Security Limits
records.learningGap: Learners may assume that any scrambled output is secure and may not distinguish demonstrating encryption/decryption from demonstrating resistance to an attacker; a tiny public-key example can expose that difference.
records.overlapCheck: No current lab teaches encryption strength or key attacks. The idea does not overlap existing labs, but it is less directly required by 0478 section 2.3 than the purpose and key-role candidates and risks turning into an RSA mathematics lesson.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 49-51

references.title: RSA Interactive | Maths Is Fun
references.teachingConnection: Useful only when small-number RSA mathematics is the intended object.

references.title: Teach teens computing: Encryption and cryptography | Raspberry Pi Foundation
references.teachingConnection: The course places simple ciphers and modern symmetric/asymmetric encryption in an age-14-to-16 teaching sequence. That supports a possible bridge from visible scrambling to modern key-based encryption, but section 2.3 itself does not require RSA arithmetic.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner encrypts a short message with a deliberately tiny public-key example, then asks the built-in eavesdropper to attempt recovery by factoring the visible modulus.
interaction.visibleChange: The receiver decrypts with the private key immediately, while the eavesdropper can also recover the message only when the toy modulus is small; a larger abstract key shows the attack becoming impractical without simulating real cryptography.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Encryption changes plaintext into ciphertext using keys, but a teaching toy is not automatically secure. Key size and the difficulty of deriving a private key matter, although RSA mathematics is outside the core 0478 section 2.3 requirement.

records.revisedDirection: Keep the idea visible, but do not automate it yet. Current depth or interaction evidence does not justify the likely implementation effort.
records.distinctGap: It distinguishes reversible scrambling from practical security, a concept absent from current labs but not explicitly required by the cited syllabus.

assessment.summary: The toy attack exposes an important misconception, but RSA factorisation and key strength are outside the core requirement and could pull attention toward mathematics rather than the purpose and roles of encryption.

interaction.visibleChange: The active state and traversed edge highlight while a current-state, input, output and next-state trace row appears.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: A state-transition diagram documents how each event changes an algorithm's state and what output occurs.

records.revisedDirection: Retain for owner review; do not recreate. The ticket-gate model already synchronizes diagram completion, current state, events, outputs and trace.
records.distinctGap: No existing lab models event-driven states or uses a state-transition diagram to document an algorithm.

assessment.summary: One four-state diagram and one fixed event sequence create a bounded prediction-and-trace loop. The CS Field Guide supplies a concrete interactive state-machine reference and the Cambridge-focused video anchors event, output and successive-state notation.

records.subject: computer-science
records.title: Symmetric Key Distribution
records.learningGap: Learners may know that symmetric encryption uses one key but fail to see why a sender and receiver who have not already shared that secret cannot safely send the key across a channel monitored by an eavesdropper.
records.overlapCheck: No existing lab models key distribution. Parity & ARQ exposes corruption and retransmission, not confidentiality or a stolen key; the reference labs do not cover encryption. This is related to the eavesdropper idea but focuses narrowly on the setup problem rather than message readability alone.

syllabusObjectives.claim: Understand the need for and purpose of encryption when transmitting data
Understand how data is encrypted using symmetric and asymmetric encryption

book.label: GCSE coursebook, printed pp. 49-51

references.title: NRICH Public Key Cryptography
references.teachingConnection: Makes Alice, Bob, Eve and key-role consequences concrete.

references.title: The Key Distribution Problem | OpenLearn, The Open University
references.teachingConnection: Frames the practical problem of sharing a symmetric secret over a watched channel.

references.title: Public key encryption | Khan Academy
references.teachingConnection: Khan Academy frames the learner's practical question: how can two computers exchange a shared symmetric key when an attacker can watch the wire? Its contrast between a shared key and public-key encryption supports a focused key-handoff puzzle.

references.title: Public Key Cryptography - Computerphile
references.teachingConnection: The video supplies a memorable public/private-key analogy that can motivate why a public key may travel openly while the private key remains with the receiver. Use only the conceptual inspiration; do not reproduce its presentation or assets.

interaction.learnerAction: Learner first sends a symmetric key openly, then reruns the same message setup using a receiver's public key to protect the secret key before sending the message.
interaction.visibleChange: Eve copies the openly sent symmetric key and can unlock subsequent ciphertext; in the second run Eve sees a public key and wrapped key but the receiver's private-key step alone reveals the shared secret.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Symmetric encryption can protect the message once both sides share a secret, but sending that secret openly defeats the protection. Asymmetric public/private keys provide a way to protect the handoff.

records.revisedDirection: Fold into the encryption workbench as a counterfactual: openly send the shared key, then protect that handoff with the receiver's public key.
records.distinctGap: It isolates secure establishment of a shared secret, an outcome not present in any current transmission, stack or memory lab.

assessment.summary: The Open University Alice/Bob/Eve sequence supports a sharp causal realization: sending a shared secret openly lets Eve decrypt later traffic. However, key distribution is an inferred extension of the cited 0478 wording and substantially overlaps the broader encryption-transmission candidate.

interaction.learnerAction: Assemble one fictional URL by choosing its protocol, domain and page/file name, then change only one part before pressing Request.

records.title: Circle Theorem Constraint Network

assessment.summary: Rank 2 of 4. Build now. A constrained circle construction lets learners move valid elements, select a theorem and observe which invariants survive; the linked hidden geometry and counterexamples require a persistent interactive surface. The current lab catalogue contains no Mathematics or 0580 lab, and the record's overlap note distinguishes adjacent 0580 candidates. records.learningGap: Learners may recognise individual circle-theorem diagrams but fail to decide which invariant applies when points move, or how E4.8 chord and tangent symmetry properties connect lengths, perpendicular bisectors and the centre to the angle theorems in E4.7.

syllabusObjectives.claim:
Calculate unknown angles and give explanations using the following geometrical properties of circles:
• angle in a semicircle = 90°
• angle between tangent and radius = 90°.
Candidates will be expected to use the geometrical properties listed in the syllabus when giving reasons for answers.

Calculate unknown angles and give explanations using the following geometrical properties of circles:
• angle in a semicircle = 90°
• angle between tangent and radius = 90°
• angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference
• angles in the same segment are equal
• opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180° (supplementary)
• alternate segment theorem.
Candidates are expected to use the geometrical properties listed in the syllabus when giving reasons for answers.

Use the following symmetry properties of circles:
• equal chords are equidistant from the centre
• the perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre
• tangents from an external point are equal in length.
Candidates are expected to use the geometrical properties listed in the syllabus when giving reasons for answers.

book.label: Morrison and Hamshaw, Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics Core and Extended, 2nd ed. (2018), printed pp. 469-482; supporting only: front matter does not print 0580 or establish 2025-2027 syllabus alignment

references.title: Circles Properties and Angle Properties of Circles
references.teachingConnection: Collects operated measurements for the E4.7 angle properties and the E4.8 chord, centre and tangent relationships, while explicitly noting that formal proof is separate.

references.title: Symmetry Properties of Circles
references.teachingConnection: Directly explores all three E4.8 properties: equal chords and centre distances, perpendicular chord bisectors, and equal tangents from an external point.

references.title: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 syllabus for 2025-2027
references.teachingConnection: Separates the Core pair, Extended Circle theorems I and the distinct E4.8 Circle theorems II symmetry-property boundary.

interaction.learnerAction: Construct a circle from constrained points, chords or tangents, predict a missing angle or length relationship and cite the theorem, then drag one permitted point to stress-test whether the claimed relationship remains invariant.
interaction.visibleChange: Angles, chord distances, perpendicular bisectors and tangent lengths update together; a correct theorem stays invariant under valid motion, while a mismatched theorem visibly loses its required conditions.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Circle theorems are conditional invariants linking the centre, circumference, chords and tangents; identifying the defining structure determines which angle or length relationship is valid.

records.revisedDirection: Use theorem-selectable constructions with conditions always visible. Preserve E4.8 as an explicit chord-and-tangent symmetry mode rather than absorbing it into generic angle questions. Exclude intersecting-chord products, secant-length theorems and any property not listed in C4.7, E4.7 or E4.8.
records.distinctGap: It connects theorem selection to invariant evidence across movable circle constructions, including the separately bounded E4.8 chord and tangent symmetry properties.

references.teachingConnection: Provides a topographic-map and coordinate-grid setting for a location task, but the actual activity uses compass bearings and triangulation rather than a perpendicular-bisector/equal-distance construction; those methods remain outside this syllabus record.

interaction.learnerAction: Set two coordinate endpoints, predict the segment length, midpoint and perpendicular gradient, construct the perpendicular-bisector equation, then test candidate points for equal distances to both endpoints.
interaction.visibleChange: Moving either endpoint changes the horizontal and vertical legs, exact length, midpoint and perpendicular bisector together; a point on the bisector shows equal endpoint distances, while an off-line point shows the inequality.
interaction.conceptualConclusion: Coordinate differences give the segment length and gradient, coordinate averages give its midpoint, and a perpendicular bisector combines a midpoint condition with a right-angle gradient and equal distances.
interaction.authenticProblem: Establish an equal-distance boundary between two surveyed reference points using only their coordinate positions.

records.revisedDirection: Use one coordinate map with two movable endpoints, a segment decomposition and a constructed perpendicular bisector. Keep the equal-distance check concrete and do not add formal loci, Voronoi diagrams, bearings or trigonometry.
